p.src: Now Sima Zhao heard that Zhuge Dan had joined forces with the troops of Wu and was coming to seek a decisive battle. He therefore summoned Pei Xiu, Senior Clerk to the Cavalier Attendants, and Zhong Hui, Gentleman Attendant at the Palace Gate, to discuss a plan for defeating the enemy. Zhong Hui said, “The troops of Wu have come to aid Zhuge Dan solely in pursuit of gain; if we lure them with gain, victory is certain.” Zhao followed his advice. He ordered Shi Bao and Zhou Tai to lead two forces ahead and lie in ambush at Shitou, with Wang Ji and Chen Qian commanding elite troops behind them, while the assistant general Cheng Cui was sent forward with tens of thousands of soldiers to entice the enemy. He further ordered Chen Jun to bring carts, oxen, horses, donkeys, and mules laden with goods intended as rewards for the army, and mass them throughout the formation, abandoning them if the enemy came.

He further ordered Chen Jun to bring carts, oxen, horses, donkeys, and mules laden with goods intended as rewards for the army, and mass them throughout the formation, abandoning them if the enemy came.

p.src: That day Zhuge Dan placed the Wu general Zhu Yi on the left and Wen Qin on the right. Seeing the men and horses in the Wei lines in disarray, Dan drove his whole force straight forward. Cheng Cui retreated, and Dan pressed his troops forward in pursuit. When they saw oxen, horses, donkeys, and mules covering the countryside, the southern soldiers scrambled to seize them and lost all desire to fight. Suddenly a cannon blast sounded, and two forces charged upon them. Shi Bao came from the left and Zhou Tai from the right. Dan was greatly alarmed. Just as he hurried to withdraw, the elite troops of Wang Ji and Chen Qian fell upon him. Dan’s army suffered a crushing defeat. Sima Zhao also led troops forward in support. Dan led his defeated troops into Shouchun, shut the gates, and held fast. Zhao ordered his soldiers to surround the city on all sides and concentrate their strength on the assault.

p.src: At this time the Wu army withdrew and encamped at Anfeng, while the emperor of Wei’s carriage halted at Xiangcheng. Zhong Hui said, “Though Zhuge Dan has now been defeated, Shouchun still holds plentiful provisions, and the Wu troops encamped at Anfeng form a supporting horn with the city. If we surround and attack from every side, they will hold firm when pressed lightly and fight to the death when pressed hard. Should the Wu army seize the moment to attack us from the other side, our forces will gain nothing. It would be better to attack on three sides, leaving the main road at the southern gate open so that the rebels may flee of their own accord. If we strike them as they flee, we shall win a complete victory. The Wu army has come from afar, so its provisions are certain to fail. I shall lead light cavalry around to their rear, and they will collapse without our having to fight.” Zhao stroked Hui’s back and said, “You are truly my Zhang Liang!” He then ordered Wang Ji to withdraw the troops from the southern gate.

p.src: Now the Wu army was encamped at Anfeng. Sun Chen summoned Zhu Yi and rebuked him: “If you cannot even relieve a single city, Shouchun, how can you hope to annex the Central Plain? If you fail again, you shall certainly be beheaded!” Zhu Yi returned to his own camp to confer with his officers. Yu Quan said, “The southern gate of Shouchun is not now under siege. I am willing to lead a force in through that gate and help Zhuge Dan defend the city. General, engage the Wei army from without, and I shall charge out from within the city. Attacking from two directions, we can defeat them.” Yi approved his proposal. Quan Yi, Quan Duan, Wen Qin, and the others all volunteered to enter the city. Together with Yu Quan, they led ten thousand troops through the southern gate into the city. The Wei troops had received no order from their commander and dared not act rashly against the enemy. They allowed the Wu army to enter the city, then reported the matter to Sima Zhao. Zhao said, “Their purpose is to attack us from within and without together with Zhu Yi and thus defeat our army.” He summoned Wang Ji and Chen Qian and instructed them: “Take five thousand troops, cut off Zhu Yi’s line of advance, and strike him from the rear.” The two men accepted the order and departed. Zhu Yi was just leading his troops forward when suddenly a great clamor arose behind him. Wang Ji came from the left and Chen Qian from the right. Their two forces charged, and the Wu army was utterly defeated. Zhu Yi returned to see Sun Chen. Chen flew into a rage and said, “What use have I for a general who suffers defeat after defeat?” He ordered the soldiers to drag Zhu Yi out and behead him. He also rebuked Quan Duan’s son Quan Yi: “Unless you drive back the Wei army, neither you nor your father need ever show yourselves before me again!” Sun Chen then returned to Jianye on his own.

p.src: Zhong Hui said to Zhao, “Now that Sun Chen has withdrawn, there are no relief forces outside. We may surround the city.” Zhao agreed and pressed his troops to tighten the siege and assault the city. Quan Yi led his troops toward Shouchun, but seeing the might of the Wei army and realizing that he had no path either forward or back, he surrendered to Sima Zhao. Zhao appointed him Assistant General. Grateful for Zhao’s favor, Yi wrote a family letter to his father Quan Duan and his uncle Quan Yi, saying that Sun Chen was inhumane and that it would be better to surrender to Wei, and had the letter shot into the city. When Yi received Quan Yi’s letter, he and Duan led several thousand men out through the opened gate and surrendered. Within the city, Zhuge Dan was sunk in anxious gloom. His advisers Jiang Ban and Jiao Yi remonstrated: “There is little grain in the city and a great multitude of soldiers, so we cannot hold out long. We should lead the forces of Wu and Chu forth and fight the Wei army in a battle to the death.” Dan was furious. “I wish to defend, yet you wish to fight. Can it be that you harbor disloyal intentions? Speak of it again and you shall be beheaded!” The two men raised their faces to heaven and sighed deeply: “Dan is doomed! We would do better to surrender early and escape death!” At the second watch that night, Jiang and Jiao climbed over the wall and surrendered to Wei, and Sima Zhao gave them important posts. Thereafter, though there were men in the city eager to fight, none dared speak of battle.

p.src: Within the city, Dan saw the Wei troops raising earthen ramparts on every side to hold back the waters of the Huai. He could only hope that a flood would wash the ramparts away, allowing him to drive his troops out against them. But contrary to expectation, from autumn through winter there was no prolonged rain, and the Huai did not flood. The city’s provisions were visibly nearing exhaustion. Wen Qin and his two sons were holding the inner fortress, but as he watched the soldiers gradually collapse from hunger, he had no choice but to tell Dan: “Our provisions are utterly exhausted, and the soldiers are being wasted by hunger. It would be better to send all the northern troops out of the city and thus reduce the mouths we must feed.” Dan was enraged. “You urge me to send away all my northern troops—are you plotting against me?” He ordered that Wen Qin be dragged out and beheaded. When Wen Yang and Wen Hu saw that their father had been killed, each drew a short sword and slew scores of men on the spot. They raced up the wall, leapt down from it, crossed the moat, and went to the Wei camp to surrender. Sima Zhao remembered with hatred how Wen Yang had once driven back his army single-handed, and wished to execute him. Zhong Hui remonstrated: “The guilt lay with Wen Qin, and Wen Qin is now dead. His two sons have come to submit because they are in desperate straits. If you kill generals who surrender, you will only harden the hearts of those within the fortified city.” Zhao accepted his counsel. He summoned Wen Yang and Wen Hu into his tent, soothed them with kindly words, bestowed fine horses and brocade robes upon them, appointed them Assistant Generals, and enfeoffed them as Marquises Within the Passes. The two brothers bowed their thanks, mounted their horses, and rode around the city shouting, “The General-in-Chief has pardoned our offenses and granted us rank. Why do you not surrender at once?” When the people within the city heard this, they all reasoned among themselves: “Wen Yang was an enemy of the Sima clan, yet even he has received an important appointment. How much more readily would they accept the likes of us?” Thus they all began to desire surrender. When Zhuge Dan heard of this, he flew into a rage and personally patrolled the walls day and night, using executions to inspire fear.

p.src: Zhong Hui knew that the hearts of those within the city had changed, so he entered Zhao’s tent and told him, “Now is the time to attack the city.” Zhao was overjoyed. He roused the three armies, which massed like clouds on every side and attacked all at once. The defending general Zeng Xuan surrendered the northern gate and let the Wei troops into the city. When Dan learned that the Wei troops had entered, he hastily led several hundred followers out by a narrow lane within the city. At the drawbridge he ran straight into Hu Zun, who raised his blade and brought it down, cutting Dan from his horse. All several hundred of his followers were captured. Wang Ji led troops to the western gate, where he encountered the Wu general Yu Quan. Ji shouted, “Why did you not surrender sooner?” Quan angrily replied, “I came forth under orders to rescue another from peril. Having failed to save him, to surrender now to someone else is something honor will not permit!” He flung his helmet to the ground and cried, “For a man living in this world, what greater fortune is there than to die upon the battlefield?” He brandished his blade and fought desperately for more than thirty bouts, until man and horse were both exhausted and he was slain amid the melee. p.src: Now most of the Wu troops had surrendered to Wei. Pei Xiu told Sima Zhao, “The families of these Wu soldiers all dwell in the southeastern lands of the Yangzi and Huai. If we keep the men here, they will surely cause trouble in time. Better to bury them alive.” Zhong Hui said, “That is not so. The ancient masters of war held that preserving a state intact was best, and executed only the chief evildoers. To bury them all alive would be inhumane. Better to release them south of the Yangzi, thereby displaying the magnanimity of the realm.” Zhao said, “An excellent argument.” He therefore released all the Wu soldiers to return to their own country. Tang Zi, fearing Sun Chen, dared not return home and instead came over to Wei. Zhao entrusted them all with important posts and stationed them throughout the region of the Three Rivers. Huainan was now pacified. Just as Zhao was preparing to withdraw, a sudden report came that Jiang Wei of western Shu was leading troops to seize the Great Wall and cut off the grain supplies. Zhao was greatly alarmed and consulted his officers on how to withdraw the army.

In Hanzhong, Jiang Wei selected two officers from Shu, Jiang Shu and Fu Qian, and drilled troops and horses with them every day. Both were notably brave, and Wei valued them highly. Suddenly came news that Zhuge Dan had risen in Huainan against Sima Zhao, aided by Sun Chen of Eastern Wu, and that Zhao had mobilized the armies of the two Huai regions and taken the Empress Dowager and the Wei emperor with him on campaign. p.src: When Jiang Wei finished reading, he flew into a rage. “This is the argument of a pedantic scholar!” he cried. He flung it to the ground. He then led the army of Shu forth to seize the Central Plain. He also asked Fu Qian, “In your judgment, by which route should we advance?” Qian replied, “Wei's stores of grain and fodder are all at the Great Wall. We should now make straight for Luo Valley. Cross Mount Shen and go directly to the Great Wall; first burn their provisions, then advance straight upon Qinchuan. The Central Plain can then be won within days.” Wei said, “Your view accords perfectly with my own plan.” He immediately led his army straight through Luo Valley, crossed Mount Shen, and advanced toward the Great Wall.

p.src: Now the general guarding the Great Wall was Sima Wang, an elder cousin of Sima Zhao. The city held abundant grain and fodder, but few troops and horses. Hearing that the Shu army was approaching, Wang hurriedly led the generals Wang Zhen and Li Peng out to encamp twenty li from the city. The next day the Shu army arrived, and Wang led the two generals out in battle array. Jiang Wei rode forward, pointed at Wang, and said, “Sima Zhao has now removed his sovereign into the army; he must harbor the same designs as Li Jue and Guo Si. I have come by the court's express command to call him to account. You should surrender at once. If you remain foolishly obstinate, your whole family will be put to death!” Wang answered loudly, “You insolent wretches! You have repeatedly invaded the superior realm. Unless you withdraw at once, I shall see that not one piece of your armor returns!” Before he had finished, Wang Zhen galloped from behind him with leveled spear, and Fu Qian rode out from the Shu ranks to meet him. Before ten bouts had passed, Qian feigned an opening, and Wang Zhen thrust his spear at him. Fu Qian dodged and captured Zhen alive in the saddle, then turned back toward his own lines. Li Peng, enraged, spurred his horse forward, whirling his blade, to rescue him. Qian deliberately slowed. When Li Peng drew near, he hurled Zhen violently to the ground and secretly readied a four-edged iron mace in his hand. Li Peng caught up and raised his blade to strike. Fu Qian twisted around and struck him once squarely in the face with the mace, bursting his eyes from their sockets and killing him beneath his horse. Wang Zhen was stabbed to death by the Shu soldiers in a flurry of spears. Jiang Wei drove his troops forward in a great advance. Sima Wang abandoned his camp, withdrew into the city, and shut the gates, refusing to come out. Wei gave orders: “Let the soldiers rest here tonight and restore their fighting spirit. Tomorrow we must enter the city.” At dawn the next day, the Shu troops vied with one another to advance and surged to the foot of the walls. They shot fire arrows and incendiary missiles into the city. The thatched buildings atop the walls caught fire everywhere, throwing the Wei troops into confusion. Wei also had dry firewood piled high beneath the walls and set ablaze all at once; the fierce flames soared to heaven. The city was on the verge of falling. Inside, the Wei soldiers wailed bitterly, their cries carrying across the countryside.

p.src: In the midst of the assault, a tremendous shout suddenly arose behind them. Wei reined in his horse and looked back to see Wei troops approaching in a mighty host, beating drums and waving banners. Wei ordered the rear ranks to become the van and stationed himself beneath the command banner to await them. From the Wei formation emerged a young officer in full armor, galloping forward with leveled spear. He looked just over twenty, his face fair as powdered jade and his lips red as vermilion. In a fierce voice he cried, “Do you know General Deng?” Wei thought, “This must be Deng Ai.” He leveled his spear and galloped forward. The two summoned all their vigor and fought thirty or forty bouts without either gaining the advantage. The young officer's spear technique did not slacken in the least. Wei thought, “Unless I use this stratagem, how can I prevail?” He wheeled his horse and fled toward a mountain path on the left. The young officer spurred after him. Wei hung up his steel spear, secretly drew his carved bow and feathered arrow, and shot at him. The young officer was sharp-eyed and had already seen it. At the twang of the bowstring, he bent forward and let the feathered arrow pass over him. Wei looked back and saw the young officer already upon him, thrusting with his spear. Wei dodged. He wished to fight Deng Ai but feared his horse was exhausted, so he pointed at Ai in feigned bravado and said, “Today I have come to know both father and son. Let each side withdraw for now; tomorrow we shall decide the battle.” Seeing that the situation on the field was unfavorable, Ai also reined in his horse and replied, “If so, let each side withdraw. A man who resorts to secret tricks is no true hero.” Thus both armies withdrew. Deng Ai encamped beside the Wei River, while Jiang Wei pitched camp astride two mountains. p.src: Now Jiang Wei sent a letter of challenge into Ai's camp, proposing a great battle the next day, and Ai pretended to accept. At the fifth watch the next morning, Wei ordered the whole army to prepare food, then formed ranks at dawn and waited. In Ai's camp, however, the banners lay furled and the drums were silent; it seemed utterly deserted. Only at evening did Wei return. The next day he sent another challenge, reproaching Ai for failing to keep the appointed time. p.src: After this had happened five or six times, Fu Jian said to Jiang Wei, “There must be some scheme behind this. We should be on our guard.” Jiang Wei replied, “They are merely waiting for the troops from Guanzhong to arrive, so they can attack us from three sides. I shall now send a letter to Sun Chen of Eastern Wu and ask him to join forces with us in attacking them.” Suddenly, a scout reported that Sima Zhao had attacked Shouchun and slain Zhuge Dan, and that all the Wu troops had surrendered.
